232.title: The most beautiful names
232.hook: to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call on Him by them (7:180)
232.howItsDone: Muslims call on Allah by the name that fits their need in du'a (ya Rahman, ya Ghafur), often learn the names as children through recited lists, and carry them in personal names like Abdullah and Abdul-Rahman.

segments.voice: Yesterday, camp four closed with hifz: seventy-five days from An-Nas back to An-Naba'. Your line was the ones every child knows. Did you say one surah by heart? Today, camp five begins. Day two hundred thirty-two.

Abdullah. Abdul-Rahman. Abdul-Karim. Abdul-Aziz. Abdul-Latif. Each of these names starts the same way, 'abd, servant of, and then comes a name of God. Servant of the Merciful. Servant of the Generous. Servant of the Mighty. Servant of the Gentle. A person can carry a name of God inside their own name for a lifetime and hardly notice it's there. So saying hi to an Abdul-Rahman means saying one of the most beautiful names out loud. Camp five is called further in, and it begins with the names. Today: al-asma' al-husna, the most beautiful names.
screen: `ABDULLAH, ABDUL-RAHMAN, ABDUL-KARIM.` → `SERVANT OF A NAME.` → `CAMP FIVE: FURTHER IN.`

segments.voice: The phrase comes straight from the Qur'an. Here is Pickthall's translation of Surah al-A'raf: Allah's are the fairest names. Invoke Him by them. Asma' is the plural of ism, name. Husna is the feminine form of ahsan, most beautiful, best, finest. The fairest names. The phrase comes back in other surahs too: at the end of al-Hashr, and in Ta Ha, and in al-Isra', where people are told they may call on Allah or call on the Most Merciful, whichever they call, His are the most beautiful names. Why names, and not a description? Muslim teaching holds that in this life Allah can't be seen, pictured or fully understood, but He can be known through what He has told people about Himself. Each name is like a window: you can't see the whole house through one window, but you can see something true. The Merciful. The Living. Peace. The Loving. And notice the verb: invoke Him by them, call on Him by them. The names aren't for a list on a wall. They're for calling. A person who is afraid might call on the Protector. A person who has done wrong calls on the Forgiving. Someone lost calls on the Guide. You've met several already. Ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim in every bismillah. Al-Wadud, the Loving, in al-Buruj. Al-Hayy and al-Qayyum in Ayat al-Kursi. For the next weeks we'll take them one at a time, a first selection, and each one will be a new way to call.
screen: `ASMA' — NAMES. HUSNA — MOST BEAUTIFUL.` · `EACH NAME A WINDOW.` · `NAMES ARE FOR CALLING.` · `THE ONES YOU'VE ALREADY MET.` · then, large: `CALL HIM BY HIS NAMES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and settle your breath. Now look for a name of Allah you already know. Maybe ar-Rahman, from the bismillah. Maybe as-Salam, peace, hidden in the greeting. Maybe al-Wadud, the Loving. Pick one. Say it slowly in your mind with each out-breath, and notice what it brings up. A feeling, a memory, a need. If you pray, you can call on Allah by that name, simply: ya Rahman, O Most Merciful. If you don't, just let the name and its meaning sit with you. The bell holds the time.
Al-asma' al-husna. The most beautiful names: the names by which Allah is known in the Qur'an, given to call on Him by. Today's word.
Your line: call him by his names. Today, when you need something, notice which name fits the need, and if you pray, call on Him by it. Day two hundred thirty-two.

233.title: Ninety-nine names
233.hook: the Prophet ﷺ said Allah has ninety-nine names and whoever learns them enters the garden (Bukhari)
233.howItsDone: Muslims often learn a recited list of the ninety-nine names as children, sometimes set to a melody, and use prayer beads of ninety-nine or thirty-three to remember Allah by His names after prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-asma' al-husna, the most beautiful names, given for calling. Your line was call him by his names. Which name fit a need yesterday? Day two hundred thirty-three.

A set of Muslim prayer beads, a misbaha, slips through the fingers one bead at a time. Count them and you may find ninety-nine, sometimes split into three groups of thirty-three by two small markers, or thirty-three, meant to go around three times. They hang from taxi mirrors in Cairo and from kitchen hooks in Dearborn. That number isn't random. It comes from a single sentence of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, recorded by both Bukhari and Muslim, with a promise attached. And scholars have turned that sentence over, lovingly, ever since: what exactly the number means, and what it means to know the names. Today: ninety-nine names.
screen: `PRAYER BEADS IN A TAXI.` → `NINETY-NINE, OR THIRTY-THREE THREE TIMES.` → `ONE SENTENCE, AND A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the hadith, in paraphrase. Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred minus one. Whoever ahsaha them will enter the Garden. And then: He is odd, witr, and He loves what is odd. Everything turns on one verb, ahsaha. At its simplest it means to count, to number off. But the scholars didn't stop at counting. Some said it means to memorize them. Others: to understand them. Others: to live by them, so that knowing the Merciful makes you merciful, and knowing the Patient makes you patient. Some said a real ahsaha holds all of these. Counting is the door. Living is the house. Then a surprise. The hadith gives the number, but not the list. The list most people learn, the one sung in schools and printed on posters, comes from a report in Tirmidhi's collection, and hadith scholars such as Ibn Hajar discussed whether the list was added by a narrator rather than spoken by the Prophet. Other early lists differ by a few names. There's even a du'a, recorded by Ahmad, asking Allah by every name He has, including names He has kept hidden in His own knowledge. So scholars such as an-Nawawi understood the hadith this way: not that Allah has only ninety-nine names, but that there are ninety-nine that come with this promise. Ninety-nine doors, and more behind them. You don't need to walk through all of them this month. We'll take a first selection.
screen: `ONE HUNDRED MINUS ONE.` · `AHSAHA — COUNT, KNOW, LIVE.` · `THE NUMBER, BUT NOT THE LIST.` · `NINETY-NINE, AND MORE BEHIND THEM.` · then, large: `NINETY-NINE DOORS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and count on your fingers the names you already know. Say each one quietly and fold a finger. Ar-Rahman. Ar-Rahim. As-Salam. Al-Wadud. Al-Hayy. Al-Qayyum. Maybe al-Ghafur, the Forgiving, or al-Karim, the Generous, from a friend's name. Don't worry about how many. When you run out, rest your hands open and breathe. Each name you counted is a door you've already found. The bell holds the time.
Ninety-nine names. The number of names the Prophet said come with the promise of the Garden, for whoever counts, knows and lives by them. Today's word.
Your line: ninety-nine doors. Today, start a list: write down every name of Allah you know so far, with a few words about what each one means. Leave room. Day two hundred thirty-three.

234.title: Allah, the name itself
234.hook: the name itself, the one proper name, holding all the others
234.howItsDone: Muslims say the name Allah throughout the day inside everyday phrases (bismillah, alhamdulillah, insha'Allah, Allahu akbar), and some repeat it on its own in dhikr, remembrance, often counting on prayer beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ninety-nine names, and the verb ahsaha: count, know, live. Your line was ninety-nine doors. How many names made it onto your list? Day two hundred thirty-four.

Bismillah. Alhamdulillah. Insha'Allah. Allahu akbar. One word sits inside every one of those phrases, and it hides so well in everyday speech that it's easy to stop hearing it. A Muslim might say it many times before lunch without once stopping to ask: what kind of word is this? It isn't like the others we're about to learn. Ar-Rahman describes. Al-Malik describes. This one names. Before the names that describe, the name itself. Today: Allah.
screen: `BISMILLAH, ALHAMDULILLAH, INSHA'ALLAH.` → `A WORD WE STOP HEARING.` → `NOT A DESCRIPTION. A NAME.`

segments.voice: Muslim scholars call Allah al-ism al-'alam, the proper name, and some call it the greatest name. The other names describe Him: Allah is the Merciful, Allah is the King. The order never runs the other way: the names are said of Allah, and Allah is the one they all belong to. That's why the Qur'an can say, at the end of al-Hashr, He is Allah, and then pour out a string of names after it. The name holds them. Where does the word come from? Here the grammarians disagree, and it's worth saying so. Some said it comes from al-ilah, the god, the two words run together, so Allah means the God, the only one. Others said it isn't derived from anything at all: it's a name, full stop, never a common noun. Both sides agree on some things. It has no plural: there are ilahs, gods, but there is no plural of Allah. It has no feminine. Grammar itself refuses to share it. It's the name in the testimony, la ilaha illa Allah, there is no god but Allah. And it isn't only a Muslim word. Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews say Allah for God, and Arabic Bibles use it. Listen, too, to how it sounds. Remember tajwid? The l in Allah is heavy and full when an a or u comes before it, as in Allahu akbar, and light after an i, as in bismillah. And the name ends in a soft h, almost just a breath.
screen: `THE PROPER NAME, NOT A DESCRIPTION.` · `THE ONE THE OTHER NAMES BELONG TO.` · `NO PLURAL, NO FEMININE.` · `IT ENDS IN A BREATH.` · then, large: `THE NAME OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and slow your breathing. On the in-breath, let the first part rise: al. On the out-breath, let the rest go: lah, and let the h at the end become just breath leaving you. Al, on the way in. Lah, on the way out. Notice how the name ends where the breath ends. If you pray, you can let this be your remembrance. If you don't, simply listen to the sound and the breath together. The bell holds the time.
Allah. The proper name of God in Arabic, with no plural and no feminine, the name all the other beautiful names belong to. Today's word.
Your line: the name of names. Today, each time you hear or say a phrase with Allah in it, bismillah, insha'Allah, stop for one second and hear the name itself. Day two hundred thirty-four.

235.title: Ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful
235.hook: the Most Merciful, whose mercy covers everything that exists
235.howItsDone: Muslims say ar-Rahman in every bismillah, and Surah ar-Rahman, with its refrain about the favors of the Lord, is often recited; Abdul-Rahman, servant of the Most Merciful, is a common name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Allah, the name itself, with no plural and ending in a breath. Your line was the name of names. Did you catch yourself hearing it inside an everyday phrase? Day two hundred thirty-five.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his companions are camped at Hudaybiyyah, outside Mecca, and a peace treaty is being written with the Quraysh, the people who drove them out. Ali holds the pen. The Prophet dictates the first words: bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim. And the Meccan envoy, Suhayl, stops him. As for ar-Rahman, he says, by God, I don't know what that is. Write in Your name, O Allah, the way you used to. The companions bristle. It's the first line of the treaty, and it's already a fight. What happens next says something about the name itself. Today: Ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful.
screen: `A TREATY AT HUDAYBIYYAH.` → `ALI HOLDS THE PEN.` → `I DON'T KNOW WHAT AR-RAHMAN IS.`

segments.voice: The Prophet said: write it as he asks. Bismika Allahumma. In Your name, O Allah. Bukhari records it. The name of mercy gave way so that peace could be written, and some readers see mercy itself in that. Why didn't Suhayl know the name? The report doesn't say, but the Qur'an records Meccans asking the same thing: and what is ar-Rahman? It comes from the root r-h-m, the root of mercy, and its form, fa'lan, is one that grammarians say Arabic uses for things that are full, overflowing, at their peak, like ghadban, full of anger, or 'atshan, full of thirst. So ar-Rahman is mercy at its fullest, mercy that fills everything. Scholars say the name belongs to Allah alone; no person is to be called ar-Rahman. And the Qur'an gives it an entire surah. Surah ar-Rahman opens with the name alone, and then lists gifts: the Qur'an taught, speech, the sun and moon in their courses, fruit, the palm with its sheaths, grain, the two seas. Thirty-one times it asks, which of the favors of your Lord will you deny? Here is how the Qur'an puts it in Surah al-A'raf, in Pickthall's translation: and My mercy embraceth all things. All things. One classical explanation reads ar-Rahman as mercy that reaches every creature in this world, whoever they are, whatever they believe: the rain falls on every field. The name's closer partner comes tomorrow.
screen: `WRITE IT AS HE ASKS.` · `WHAT IS AR-RAHMAN?` · `FA'LAN — FULL, OVERFLOWING.` · `MY MERCY EMBRACETH ALL THINGS.` · then, large: `MERCY COVERS ALL.`

segments.voice: Sit, and open your eyes softly. For one minute, look for mercy. Not the dramatic kind. The light coming through a window. The chair holding you up. The air arriving in your lungs without being asked. Your heart doing its work while you weren't paying attention. Name each one silently as you find it. Then close your eyes and let the list keep going on its own. If you pray, you can say, ya Rahman, softly, at the end. The bell holds the time.
Ar-Rahman. The Most Merciful, mercy at its fullest, overflowing onto everything that exists, a name used only for Allah. Today's word.
Your line: mercy covers all. Today, when you're tempted to think someone is outside of every mercy, remember the rain falling on every field. Day two hundred thirty-five.

236.title: Ar-Rahim, the Most Compassionate
236.hook: the Most Compassionate, mercy that reaches each one, closely
236.howItsDone: Muslims say ar-Rahim with ar-Rahman in every bismillah, and many take the hadith of the merciful being shown mercy as a daily rule: kindness to family, neighbors, strangers and animals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ar-Rahman: mercy overflowing, and a treaty where the name gave way for peace. Your line was mercy covers all. Where did you notice it falling on every field? Day two hundred thirty-six.

After a battle, captives are brought into Medina. Among them is a woman who is frantic, searching every face, every corner. She has lost her baby. Whenever she finds a small child among the captives, she lifts it, presses it to her chest and feeds it, again and again. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is watching with his companions, and Bukhari and Muslim record what he asked them: do you think this woman would ever throw her child into a fire? They said, no, never, not if she could help it. Yesterday was mercy like the rain, falling on everything. Today is mercy like that mother's arms. Today: Ar-Rahim, the Most Compassionate.
screen: `A MOTHER SEARCHING EVERY FACE.` → `ANY CHILD, HELD CLOSE.` → `WOULD SHE THROW IT IN A FIRE?`

segments.voice: The Prophet said: Allah is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her child. Ar-Rahim comes from the same root as ar-Rahman, r-h-m, and they almost always travel together: bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim, in every surah but one. So why two names from one root? Scholars have given several answers, and they fit together. The form of ar-Rahman means full and overflowing. The form of ar-Rahim, fa'il, means ongoing, the one who keeps on doing it, again and again. So ar-Rahman is mercy as vast as the sky; ar-Rahim is mercy that arrives, that reaches this particular person, today. Many commentators add a second difference: ar-Rahman is mercy for all creation in this world, and ar-Rahim is a special mercy for the believers, especially in the next. The Qur'an says in al-Ahzab that He is ever merciful to the believers, rahim. Here's a surprise. Unlike ar-Rahman, the word rahim can describe a person. In Surah at-Tawbah the Prophet himself is called ra'uf rahim, kind and merciful to the believers. That makes Ar-Rahim a name you can imitate, and the Prophet said so. In Tirmidhi's collection: the merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Have mercy on those on the earth, and the One above will have mercy on you. Mercy close up isn't an idea. It's a mother holding a child close. It's someone showing up.
screen: `MORE MERCIFUL THAN THIS MOTHER.` · `ONE ROOT, TWO NAMES.` · `VAST AS THE SKY; ARRIVING TODAY.` · `A MERCY YOU CAN IMITATE.` · then, large: `MERCY CLOSE UP.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring one person to mind. Someone who could use a little mercy today. Maybe they're struggling. Maybe they're tired, or alone, or carrying something nobody sees. Picture their face. Now picture one small, specific thing you could do for them: a message, a coffee, not correcting them this once, letting them go first. Keep it tiny and real. Hold that picture for a few breaths. If you pray, you can ask ar-Rahim for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Ar-Rahim. The Most Compassionate: mercy that keeps on arriving, reaching each one closely, and a mercy people are asked to imitate. Today's word.
Your line: mercy close up. Today, do the small, specific thing for the person you pictured, and don't tell anyone you did it. Day two hundred thirty-six.

237.title: Mercy outruns anger
237.hook: Allah wrote, My mercy prevails over My anger (Bukhari; Muslim)
237.howItsDone: The hadith that Allah's mercy prevails over His anger is quoted to encourage hope and forgiveness, and the hundred parts of mercy turn up in sermons and in teaching children kindness to people and animals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ar-Rahim: mercy that keeps arriving, and a mercy people can imitate. Your line was mercy close up. Did you do the small thing for the person you pictured? Day two hundred thirty-seven.

Watch a horse with a newborn foal. The foal is wobbly, all legs, tangled up underneath her. And the mare, a huge animal, lifts one hoof and holds it in the air, carefully, so she won't step on her baby. It's a small, ordinary thing, easy to miss. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ used exactly that picture, the lifted hoof, to explain where mercy comes from. And alongside it, Bukhari and Muslim record another saying, about something written before anything else existed, about which comes first when mercy and anger meet. Two names from the root r-h-m. Now the root itself. Today: rahmah, mercy.
screen: `A MARE LIFTS HER HOOF.` → `SO SHE WON'T STEP ON HER FOAL.` → `WHICH COMES FIRST, MERCY OR ANGER?`

segments.voice: First, the writing. The Prophet said that when Allah created the creation, He wrote in a Book that is with Him, above the Throne: My mercy prevails over My anger. The reports use two different verbs, and both are worth hearing. In one, ghalabat: My mercy overcomes My anger, wins against it. In the other, sabaqat: My mercy outruns My anger, gets there first, like a runner leaving the other behind. Mercy is stronger, and it's faster. Then the hoof. In another hadith the Prophet said Allah made mercy in one hundred parts. He kept ninety-nine with Himself and sent one part down to the earth. From that one part, every creature is merciful to every other: parents to children, friend to friend, and the mare lifting her hoof from her foal. Everything tender you have ever seen in this world, all of it together, is one percent. Now the root. Rahmah, mercy, comes from r-h-m, and the same root gives rahim, the womb. Bukhari records a saying that the womb, rahim, is a branch of ar-Rahman. Some readers hear in that root a mercy shaped like the place where a person is first held, protected, and fed before they can do anything to deserve it. Muslims also believe Allah's anger is real, and the Qur'an speaks of it. The saying doesn't erase it. It puts it in order: when the two meet, mercy wins, and mercy got there first.
screen: `WRITTEN ABOVE THE THRONE.` · `GHALABAT, SABAQAT — WINS, OUTRUNS.` · `ONE PART OF A HUNDRED.` · `RAHMAH AND RAHIM, THE WOMB.` · then, large: `MERCY WINS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone who has annoyed you recently. Notice the judgment arrive: the little story about what kind of person they are. Now, before finishing that story, let mercy get there first. Picture them as someone's child, once held and fed before they'd done anything at all. Or picture the mare, lifting her hoof. You don't have to agree with them. Just let mercy run ahead of the verdict for one breath, then another. The bell holds the time.
Rahmah. Mercy, from the root that also gives the womb: the mercy Allah wrote prevails over His anger. Today's word.
Your line: mercy wins. Today, when you feel a judgment forming about someone, let forgiveness start the race first, even if judgment catches up later. Day two hundred thirty-seven.

238.title: Al-Malik, the King
238.hook: the King, owner of everything, and so nothing is really yours
238.howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un (we belong to Allah and to Him we return) at news of any loss, from a death to a broken cup, and wealth, family and life are often spoken of as an amanah, a trust held for a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rahmah: mercy in a hundred parts, one sent to earth, and mercy that outruns anger. Your line was mercy wins. Did forgiveness get to the starting line first? Day two hundred thirty-eight.

A library book can go everywhere with a person for three weeks. A corner gets folded, maybe, with a twinge of guilt. It gets read in bed and on the bus. It starts to feel like theirs. Then the due date comes, and it goes back, because it never was. In Medina, a woman named Umm Sulaym lost her little son while her husband, Abu Talha, was away. When he came home, she fed him and let him rest. Then, as the report in Sahih Muslim tells it, she asked him a question: if people lent something to a family, and then asked for it back, would the family have the right to refuse? Today: Al-Malik, the King.
screen: `A LIBRARY BOOK, DUE BACK.` → `UMM SULAYM'S QUESTION.` → `CAN YOU REFUSE TO RETURN A LOAN?`

segments.voice: No, said Abu Talha. Then, she said, seek your reward with Allah for your son. He was upset that she had waited to tell him, and he went to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who prayed for blessing on the two of them. The picture behind her question is the name we're learning. Al-Malik comes from the root m-l-k, to own, to possess, to rule. The same root gives malik, king, and mulk, sovereignty, and in the Fatiha there are two accepted readings of one line: Maliki yawm id-din, King of the Day of Judgment, and Maaliki, Owner of it. Both are recited, and the two meanings are held together. The Qur'an names Him al-Malik in al-Hashr. Here is Pickthall: He is Allah, than Whom there is no other God, the Sovereign Lord. And in an-Nas, the King of mankind. Bukhari and Muslim record the Prophet describing the Day when Allah will fold up the heavens and take the earth in His hand, and say: I am the King. Where are the kings of the earth? Every crown and every title, gone quiet. If He is the Owner, then what we call mine is held on loan: the house, the phone, the body, even the children we love. That's not meant to make things cheap. A borrowed thing is treated with care. It's meant to loosen the grip. Muslims say at any loss, in words from al-Baqarah that Pickthall renders: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning. This week began with the beautiful names, the name of names, and mercy vast and near. It ends with the King.
screen: `SEEK YOUR REWARD FOR YOUR SON.` · `M-L-K — TO OWN, TO RULE.` · `WHERE ARE THE KINGS OF THE EARTH?` · `WHAT'S MINE IS HELD ON LOAN.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING IS LENT.`

segments.voice: Pick up something small that you think of as yours. Your phone, your keys, a ring, a cup. Hold it in your open hand and look at it. Say quietly: this is lent to me. Notice what happens in your chest. Maybe a little resistance. Maybe some relief. Then set it down gently, and rest your hands on your own knees, and notice that your hands are lent too. If you pray, you can say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. The bell holds the time.
Al-Malik. The King, the Owner of everything, so that all we hold is lent, to be cared for and one day returned. Today's word.

Your line: everything is lent. Today, when you catch yourself gripping something, a possession, a plan, an argument, hold it like a library book: with care, and ready to give back. Day two hundred thirty-eight.
